title: The World’s Last Chance for Peace
gist: Spanish Prime Minister Pedro Sánchez argues the world is normalizing war (65 state-involved conflicts in 2025, defense spending up 40%+ in a decade to ~$3 trillion, nuclear buildups) and proposes 'maxilateralism': raising the costs of aggression, refusing to enable belligerents, prioritizing social over excessive defense spending, and reforming the UN Security Council, IMF/World Bank, nuclear regimes and the ICC.

themes.theme: Data on the normalization of war

insights.claim: According to the Uppsala Conflict Data Program, there were 65 active conflicts involving governments in 2025, double the 2010 number, with an estimated 250,000 deaths, the highest annual toll in 30 years.
insights.speaker: Pedro Sánchez
insights.so_what: Structural rise in conflict supports defense-sector and commodity risk premia.
insights.quote: there were 65 active conflicts involving governments in 2025, double the number in 2010
insights.locator: Today, however, there is more armed conflict

insights.claim: Global defense spending has risen more than 40% in the past decade to nearly $3 trillion a year, close to Africa's entire GDP, with traditionally restrained countries like Denmark, Germany, Japan and Norway rearming rapidly.
insights.speaker: Pedro Sánchez
insights.so_what: Confirms a multi-year defense capex cycle in Europe and Japan.
insights.quote: The nearly $3 trillion the world spends annually on defense is close to the GDP of the entire African continent
insights.locator: There is no sign of the trend

insights.claim: China's nuclear arsenal is estimated to have grown from 200-300 warheads in the late 2010s to 620 in 2026, North Korea's from 10-20 in 2018 to around 60, and in March France announced its first warhead stockpile increase since 1992.
insights.speaker: Pedro Sánchez
insights.so_what: Broad nuclear modernization sustains strategic weapons budgets.
insights.quote: France announced the first increase in its nuclear warhead stockpile since 1992
insights.locator: A renewed threat of nuclear war

insights.claim: Close to 120 million people worldwide have been forcibly displaced by war, and in 2025 at least one civilian died in armed conflict every 14 minutes per UN records.
insights.speaker: Pedro Sánchez
insights.so_what: Displacement fuels migration politics in Europe.
insights.locator: Today, however, there is more armed conflict

insights.claim: Sánchez argues AI integration into nuclear technologies is an existential threat because it compresses decision time for human judgment, and AI in biotech lowers barriers to bioweapons.
insights.speaker: Pedro Sánchez
insights.so_what: Supports regulatory push on military AI; relevant to AI governance risk.
insights.quote: as AI speeds up decision-making, it reduces the time available for human judgment
insights.locator: The integration of AI into nuclear technologies

insights.claim: Sánchez frames the core danger as countries building instruments of catastrophe at the speed of innovation while instruments of control move at the slower pace of diplomacy.
insights.speaker: Pedro Sánchez
insights.so_what: Expect regulation to lag weapons tech.
insights.quote: Countries are building the instruments of catastrophe at the blinding speed of innovation

themes.theme: Costs and spillovers of the Iran war

insights.claim: The US and Israeli war with Iran has severely disrupted maritime trade and air traffic, driving up prices of energy, fertilizer and other commodities.
insights.speaker: Pedro Sánchez
insights.so_what: Iran war is an inflationary commodity shock (energy, fertilizer).
insights.quote: driving up the prices of energy, fertilizer, and other commodities

insights.claim: Since February 2026, Iran has struck targets in several Gulf countries and other neighbors, and the war has reignited conflicts in Iraq, Lebanon and Yemen.
insights.speaker: Pedro Sánchez
insights.so_what: Gulf infrastructure risk persists; regional spillover sustains oil risk premium.
insights.quote: Since February 2026, Iran has struck targets in several Gulf countries

insights.claim: Spain denied the United States use of its territory and facilities for the war against Iran this year and has maintained an arms embargo on Israel since 2023.
insights.speaker: Pedro Sánchez
insights.so_what: Signals transatlantic friction; Spain-US relations risk (bases, trade).
insights.quote: denied the United States the use of its territory and facilities for the war against Iran

insights.claim: Spain opted out of NATO's proposed 5%-of-GDP defense spending target, though Sánchez says his government tripled net defense spending over his eight years in office.
insights.speaker: Pedro Sánchez
insights.so_what: Spain will remain a laggard on NATO spending; less upside for Spanish defense procurement vs peers.
insights.quote: opt out of NATO’s proposed defense spending target of five percent of GDP
insights.locator: Investing in prosperity is also essential

insights.claim: By keeping defense spending proportionate, Spain says it preserved fiscal space for an additional 145 billion euros in social protection, housing, health and education, and more than 30 billion euros for the green transition.
insights.speaker: Pedro Sánchez
insights.so_what: Spanish fiscal priorities favor social and green spending — relevant to sector exposure in Spain.
insights.quote: an additional 145 billion euros in social protection, housing, health care, and education
insights.locator: Investing in prosperity is also essential

insights.claim: Sánchez argues that military deterrence and social welfare must reinforce each other, since security is strengthened by resilient societies and reduced inequality.
insights.speaker: Pedro Sánchez
insights.so_what: A dissenting European voice against maximal rearmament budgets.
insights.quote: military deterrence and social welfare must reinforce each other
insights.locator: Investing in prosperity is also essential

insights.claim: Three of four Spaniards identify war as their greatest fear, and an even greater share believe another world war is on the horizon.
insights.speaker: Pedro Sánchez
insights.so_what: Domestic opinion supports Spain's restraint posture.
insights.quote: three of four Spaniards identify war as their greatest fear

insights.claim: Sánchez proposes 'maxilateralism'—cooperation embracing as many countries as possible—as superior to minilateral coalitions of the willing, which he argues further fragment the international order.
insights.speaker: Pedro Sánchez
insights.so_what: Signals Spain/EU-south preference for UN-centric diplomacy over ad hoc blocs.
insights.quote: What is needed is not minilateralism but maxilateralism.

insights.claim: Sánchez calls for expanding elected UN Security Council membership with longer terms, seats for Africa, Latin America and regional bodies like the EU and African Union, strict limits on vetoes over atrocities, and ultimately abolishing the veto.
insights.speaker: Pedro Sánchez
insights.so_what: Low near-term probability; signals reform pressure in UN secretary-general selection.
insights.quote: Ultimately, the veto should be abolished outright.

insights.claim: Sánchez argues the convention that a European leads the IMF and an American leads the World Bank must end, with more voting power for emerging economies.
insights.speaker: Pedro Sánchez
insights.so_what: Watch Bretton Woods governance reform debates.

insights.claim: Sánchez calls for a US-Russia New START successor including China, ratification of the Comprehensive Nuclear Test Ban Treaty, a Fissile Material Cutoff Treaty, and rules preserving human control over nuclear launch decisions with AI.
insights.speaker: Pedro Sánchez
insights.so_what: Arms control agenda unlikely near-term; supports defense-spending persistence.

insights.claim: Sánchez proposes that states sheltering ICC-indicted individuals face legal, diplomatic and financial consequences, opposing efforts to dismantle the International Criminal Court.
insights.speaker: Pedro Sánchez
insights.so_what: Potential friction with US/Israel over ICC enforcement.
insights.quote: States that shelter individuals indicted by the ICC should face legal, diplomatic, and financial consequences.

insights.claim: Sánchez frames development finance—debt-for-development swaps, the Debt Suspension Clause Alliance, and Spain's up to 60 million euros a year in debt relief—as peacebuilding policy.
insights.speaker: Pedro Sánchez
entities: Global Hub on Debt for Development Swaps
insights.so_what: Supports growth of debt-pause clauses and debt-swap instruments in frontier sovereign debt.
insights.quote: These development policies are peacebuilding policies, too.
